original_abstract: Omnidirectional scene text detection has received increasing research attention. Previous methods directly predict words or text lines of quadrilateral shapes. However, most methods neglect the significance of consistent labeling, which is important to maintain a stable training process, especially when a large amount of data are included. For the first time, we solve the problem in this paper by proposing a novel method termed Sequential-free Box Discretization (SBD). The proposed SBD first discretizes the quadrilateral box into several key edges, which contains all potential horizontal and vertical positions. In order to decode accurate vertex positions, a simple yet effective matching procedure is proposed to reconstruct the quadrilateral bounding boxes. It departs from the learning ambiguity which has a significant influence during the learning process. Exhaustive ablation studies have been conducted to quantitatively validate the effectiveness of our proposed method. More importantly, built upon SBD, we provide a detailed analysis of the impact of a collection of refinements, in the hope to inspire others to build state-of-the-art networks. Combining both SBD and these useful refinements, we achieve state-of-the-art performance on various benchmarks, including ICDAR 2015, and MLT. Our method also wins the first place in text detection task of the recent ICDAR2019 Robust Reading Challenge on Reading Chinese Text on Signboard, further demonstrating its powerful generalization ability. Code is available at this https URL.
generated_abstract: Scene text in natural images exhibits substantial variation in orientation, scale, aspect ratio, and geometric shape, posing challenges for accurate and efficient text spotting. We present a unified end-to-end framework that combines single-shot direct regression with instance-aware region segmentation and adaptive boundary representation for detecting and recognizing both quadrilateral and curved text. A fully convolutional backbone predicts text confidence, geometric boundaries, and corner-based localization cues, while deformable region pooling and adaptive recurrent boundary refinement provide precise representations for irregular text instances. An RoI masking module extracts shape-aware features, which are decoded by an attention-based recognizer without requiring explicit rectification. The proposed design minimizes proposal aggregation and handcrafted post-processing, retaining the speed advantages of one-stage detectors while improving localization of long, multi-oriented, and curved text. Experiments on ICDAR2013, ICDAR2015, MSRA-TD500, COCO-Text, CTW1500, and Total-Text demonstrate robust detection and end-to-end recognition across constrained and unconstrained scenes, offering an effective balance between accuracy, geometric flexibility, and inference efficiency.

original_abstract: Conventional cross-domain image-to-image translation or unsupervised domain adaptation methods assume that the source domain and target domain are closely related. This neglects a practical scenario where the domain discrepancy between the source and target is excessively large. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to learn domain adaptive features between the largely-gapped source and target domains with unlabeled domain bridges. Firstly, we introduce the framework of Cycle-consistency Flow Generative Adversarial Networks (CFGAN) that utilizes domain bridges to perform image-to-image translation between two distantly distributed domains. Secondly, we propose the Prototypical Adversarial Domain Adaptation (PADA) model which utilizes unlabeled bridge domains to align feature distribution between source and target with a large discrepancy. Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments are conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed models.
generated_abstract: We present a unified unsupervised domain adaptation framework for robust visual recognition under heterogeneous multi-source and unlabeled target domains. The method combines pixel-level adversarial translation with feature-level adaptation: source images are transformed toward the target appearance while preserving task semantics, and representations are aligned across multiple network layers using joint distribution and moment matching. To prevent over-alignment and class-boundary ambiguity, task-specific classifiers provide discrepancy-based feedback that guides target features toward the source support. A disentangled representation further separates domain-specific variation from class-relevant information, while soft label-distribution matching enables transfer across related tasks when target annotations are unavailable. The framework supports multiple labeled sources, arbitrary target domains, and large visual shifts, including synthetic-to-real and cross-modality settings. We evaluate it on standard multi-domain image classification and segmentation benchmarks, demonstrating improved transferability, class discrimination, and robustness compared with conventional adversarial, kernel-based, and single-source adaptation methods.

original_abstract: The revolution in computer hardware, especially in graphics processing units and tensor processing units, has enabled significant advances in computer graphics and artificial intelligence algorithms. In addition to their many beneficial applications in daily life and business, computer-generated/manipulated images and videos can be used for malicious purposes that violate security systems, privacy, and social trust. The deepfake phenomenon and its variations enable a normal user to use his or her personal computer to easily create fake videos of anybody from a short real online video. Several countermeasures have been introduced to deal with attacks using such videos. However, most of them are targeted at certain domains and are ineffective when applied to other domains or new attacks. In this paper, we introduce a capsule network that can detect various kinds of attacks, from presentation attacks using printed images and replayed videos to attacks using fake videos created using deep learning. It uses many fewer parameters than traditional convolutional neural networks with similar performance. Moreover, we explain, for the first time ever in the literature, the theory behind the application of capsule networks to the forensics problem through detailed analysis and visualization.
generated_abstract: We present a robust and efficient framework for detecting manipulated facial content in images and videos under diverse presentation and distribution conditions. The proposed system combines a compact convolutional feature extractor with domain-specific face preprocessing, temporal recurrent aggregation, and an unsupervised adversarial-invariance module that suppresses nuisance factors such as compression, illumination, identity, and capture device. A multi-task decoder jointly performs binary forgery classification, manipulated-region localization, and input reconstruction, encouraging representations that capture both global inconsistencies and local forensic artifacts. The framework is trained and evaluated on large-scale FaceForensics and FaceForensics++ data containing DeepFakes, Face2Face, FaceSwap, and NeuralTextures, with additional presentation attacks and cross-dataset tests assessing generalization. Experimental results demonstrate reliable detection across compression levels and video qualities, improved robustness to unseen manipulation methods and domain mismatch, accurate localization of forged regions, and substantially lower computational cost than conventional deep detectors. These results indicate that integrating spatial, temporal, and adversarially invariant cues provides a practical solution for real-world facial media authentication and forgery analysis.

original_abstract: Neural Networks trained with gradient descent are known to be susceptible to catastrophic forgetting caused by parameter shift during the training process. In the context of Neural Machine Translation (NMT) this results in poor performance on heterogeneous datasets and on sub-tasks like rare phrase translation. On the other hand, non-parametric approaches are immune to forgetting, perfectly complementing the generalization ability of NMT. However, attempts to combine non-parametric or retrieval based approaches with NMT have only been successful on narrow domains, possibly due to over-reliance on sentence level retrieval. We propose a novel n-gram level retrieval approach that relies on local phrase level similarities, allowing us to retrieve neighbors that are useful for translation even when overall sentence similarity is low. We complement this with an expressive neural network, allowing our model to extract information from the noisy retrieved context. We evaluate our semi-parametric NMT approach on a heterogeneous dataset composed of WMT, IWSLT, JRC-Acquis and OpenSubtitles, and demonstrate gains on all 4 evaluation sets. The semi-parametric nature of our approach opens the door for non-parametric domain adaptation, demonstrating strong inference-time adaptation performance on new domains without the need for any parameter updates.
generated_abstract: We present a retrieval- and phrase-guided neural machine translation framework that combines the fluency and contextual modeling of Transformer-based NMT with the adequacy and lexical coverage of phrase-based translation. For each input sentence, a search engine retrieves similar bilingual examples from the training corpus, while a document-level context encoder provides discourse information for resolving terminology and consistency. Source–target alignments are used to extract translation pieces and candidate phrases, which are incorporated into an attention-based hybrid beam search and scored jointly with neural probabilities, phrase translation features, and a target language model. A neural system-combination module further integrates independently generated NMT and phrase-based hypotheses. This design directly addresses domain mismatch, rare words, long-range dependencies, alignment errors, and the limited adequacy of purely neural decoding without requiring large document-level corpora. Experiments across general- and narrow-domain translation tasks show consistent improvements over strong Transformer baselines and individual retrieval- or phrase-enhanced systems, with the largest gains observed for repeated terminology, low-frequency expressions, and discourse-dependent translations. Analysis of retrieved examples and attention alignments demonstrates that the proposed model selectively exploits relevant translation evidence while preserving the fluency of neural generation.

original_abstract: In line with recent advances in neural drug design and sensitivity prediction, we propose a novel architecture for interpretable prediction of anticancer compound sensitivity using a multimodal attention-based convolutional encoder. Our model is based on the three key pillars of drug sensitivity: compounds’ structure in the form of a SMILES sequence, gene expression profiles of tumors and prior knowledge on intracellular interactions from protein-protein interaction networks. We demonstrate that our multiscale convolutional attention-based encoder significantly outperforms a baseline model trained on Morgan fingerprints, a selection of encoders based on SMILES as well as previously reported state of the art for multimodal drug sensitivity prediction (R2 = 0.86 and RMSE = 0.89). Moreover, the explainability of our approach is demonstrated by a thorough analysis of the attention weights. generated_abstract: We present an interpretable multimodal framework for cancer drug response prediction that integrates molecular drug structure, cancer-cell molecular profiles, pathway activity, and heterogeneous drug–target and protein-interaction networks. Drug–cell pairs are modeled as links in a unified graph, while attention-based encoders learn informative genes, pathways, atoms, and bonds. A shared multitask architecture jointly predicts continuous sensitivity and sensitive/resistant associations across drugs, enabling transfer of information between related compounds and cell contexts. Network-derived profiles and drug-induced transcriptional signatures provide complementary functional representations, improving robustness to missing and sparsely measured omics data. We evaluate the framework using cross-validation, leave-drug-out and leave-cell-line-out settings, and independent datasets, comparing it with regression, kernel, network, and deep-learning baselines. In addition to improved prediction of response, the model identifies molecular determinants and drug–pathway interactions associated with sensitivity, supports estimation of unmeasured drug responses, and prioritizes repurposing candidates for specific cancer subtypes. This application demonstrates how combining multimodal attention, heterogeneous network learning, and multitask prediction can support accurate, biologically interpretable, and clinically relevant precision oncology.

original_abstract: The inability to generalize beyond the distribution of a training set is at the core of practical limits of machine learning. We show that the common practice of mixing and shuffling training examples when training deep neural networks is not optimal. On the opposite, partitioning the training data into non-i.i.d. subsets can serve to guide the model to rely on reliable statistical patterns while ignoring spurious correlations in the training data. We demonstrate multiple use cases where these subsets are built using unsupervised clustering, prior knowledge, or other meta-data from existing datasets. The approach is supported by recent results on a causal view of generalization, it is simple to apply, and it demonstrably improves generalization. Applied to the task of visual question answering, we obtain state-of-the-art performance on VQA-CP. We also show improvements over data augmentation using equivalent questions on GQA. Finally, we show a small improvement when training a model simultaneously on VQA v2 and Visual Genome, treating them as two distinct environments rather than one aggregated training set.
generated_abstract: Visual question answering (VQA) systems often exploit language and dataset priors rather than grounding their predictions in image content, resulting in poor robustness under distribution shifts. We present a unified bias-aware VQA framework that combines counterfactual training pairs, explicit visual–semantic disentanglement, and adversarial unimodal regularization. A question-only branch estimates language-driven evidence and dynamically suppresses predictions that can be made without the image, while pairwise score regularization encourages the model to distinguish visually contrasting examples with identical or similar questions. The architecture separately models visual concept recognition and question-conditioned answer selection, improving interpretability and enabling counterexample-based explanations. We further introduce a grounding sensitivity measure that quantifies the contribution of image information to each prediction. Experiments across standard VQA, balanced VQA, and changing-prior benchmarks show that the proposed approach substantially reduces language-prior reliance, improves accuracy under shifted answer distributions, and retains competitive performance on conventional test sets. Qualitative analyses demonstrate more faithful attention and increased confidence changes between complementary images, indicating that the framework makes visual evidence central to answering.

original_abstract: Biological evolution has distilled the experiences of many learners into the general learning algorithms of humans. Our novel meta reinforcement learning algorithm MetaGenRL is inspired by this process. MetaGenRL distills the experiences of many complex agents to meta-learn a low-complexity neural objective function that affects how future individuals will learn. Unlike recent meta-RL algorithms, MetaGenRL can generalize to new environments that are entirely different from those used for meta-training. In some cases, it even outperforms human-engineered RL algorithms. MetaGenRL uses off-policy second-order gradients during meta-training that greatly increase its sample efficiency.
generated_abstract: We present a unified meta-learning framework for sample-efficient reinforcement learning that jointly learns how agents optimize, explore, and adapt. The framework represents the inner learning procedure as a recurrent algorithm whose state summarizes interaction history, while an outer loop meta-learns its update loss, value-return parameters, and intrinsic-reward mechanism across a distribution of tasks. This combines learned optimizers, meta-gradient adaptation, recurrent fast reinforcement learning, and programmatic curiosity search within a model-agnostic architecture compatible with gradient-based policies and critics. The resulting agent can rapidly infer task structure from a small number of trials, adjust bootstrapping and discounting online, and generate exploration bonuses suited to the current environment. Across few-shot visual navigation, sparse-reward control, and domain-shifted benchmark tasks, the proposed method improves early learning speed and final performance over standard policy-gradient, recurrent meta-RL, manually designed curiosity, and fixed-return baselines. Ablation studies show complementary contributions from learned optimization, adaptive returns, and intrinsic motivation, while evaluation on unseen dynamics and architectures demonstrates transfer beyond the meta-training distribution.

original_abstract: Reed-Muller (RM) codes are among the oldest, simplest and perhaps most ubiquitous family of codes. They are used in many areas of coding theory in both electrical engineering and computer science. Yet, many of their important properties are still under investigation. This paper covers some of the recent developments regarding the weight enumerator and the capacity-achieving properties of RM codes, as well as some of the algorithmic developments. In particular, the paper discusses the recent connections established between RM codes, thresholds of Boolean functions, polarization theory, hypercontractivity, and the techniques of approximating low weight codewords using lower degree polynomials. It then overviews some of the algorithms with performance guarantees, as well as some of the algorithms with state-of-the-art performances in practical regimes. Finally, the paper concludes with a few open problems.
generated_abstract: We present a symmetry-aware decoding framework for Reed–Muller and polar-derived codes that combines polarization-based construction with recursive projection–aggregation and observation-adaptive minimum-weight parity checks. The proposed method selects information coordinates using an RM–polar interpolation rule, while exploiting the resulting code’s affine symmetry through recursive projections and a dynamically pruned set of minimum-weight dual checks. This design preserves the parallelism and low implementation complexity of recursive decoding, while improving reliability through complementary soft-information aggregation and iterative constraint processing. We evaluate the framework on binary erasure, binary symmetric, and additive white Gaussian noise channels over practical block lengths and rates, comparing it with successive-cancellation list, belief-propagation, parity-check, and conventional recursive RM decoders. The results demonstrate consistent finite-length gains, with performance approaching maximum-likelihood decoding in short- to moderate-length, low- and medium-rate regimes, at substantially lower complexity than exhaustive decoding. The study further shows that combining polarization-guided reliability selection with RM symmetry provides a flexible path toward capacity-oriented constructions and practical near-ML decoding across symmetric binary-input channels.

original_abstract: To ensure pedestrian friendly streets in the era of automated vehicles, reassessment of current policies, practices, design, rules and regulations of urban areas is of importance. This study investigates pedestrian crossing behaviour, as an important element of urban dynamics that is expected to be affected by the presence of automated vehicles. For this purpose, an interpretable machine learning framework is proposed to explore factors affecting pedestrians' wait time before crossing mid-block crosswalks in the presence of automated vehicles. To collect rich behavioural data, we developed a dynamic and immersive virtual reality experiment, with 180 participants from a heterogeneous population in 4 different locations in the Greater Toronto Area (GTA). Pedestrian wait time behaviour is then analyzed using a data-driven Cox Proportional Hazards (CPH) model, in which the linear combination of the covariates is replaced by a flexible non-linear deep neural network. The proposed model achieved a 5% improvement in goodness of fit, but more importantly, enabled us to incorporate a richer set of covariates. A game theoretic based interpretability method is used to understand the contribution of different covariates to the time pedestrians wait before crossing. Results show that the presence of automated vehicles on roads, wider lane widths, high density on roads, limited sight distance, and lack of walking habits are the main contributing factors to longer wait times. Our study suggested that, to move towards pedestrian-friendly urban areas, national level educational programs for children, enhanced safety measures for seniors, promotion of active modes of transportation, and revised traffic rules and regulations should be considered.
generated_abstract: This study presents an interpretable deep-survival framework for modeling pedestrian crossing decisions and waiting times in interactions with automated vehicles (AVs). Building on research on nonverbal driver–pedestrian communication, gap acceptance, pedestrian trust, and external human–machine interfaces (eHMIs), the framework combines time-to-collision, vehicle behavior and size, pedestrian gaze, crosswalk context, traffic signals, demographics, and eHMI characteristics within a neural Cox proportional-hazards model. Data are collected through an immersive virtual-reality stated-preference experiment that enables controlled variation of yielding behavior, eHMI type and timing, and mixed-traffic conditions while preserving realistic interaction and behavioral measurement. Embedded feature selection identifies influential predictors, and model ensembles and behavioral regularization improve the stability of estimated effects. Beyond predictive performance, the model yields interpretable survival probabilities, feature effects, and heterogeneous crossing responses, allowing assessment of when communication increases perceived safety and crossing efficiency without encouraging unsafe behavior. The application demonstrates how deep learning can capture nonlinear and interactive pedestrian responses while supporting behaviorally meaningful interpretation, offering a practical tool for designing AV communication strategies and pedestrian-oriented urban infrastructure.

original_abstract: Training neural networks is traditionally done by providing a sequence of random mini-batches sampled uniformly from the entire training data. In this work, we analyze the effect of curriculum learning, which involves the non-uniform sampling of mini-batches, on the training of deep networks, and specifically CNNs trained for image recognition. To employ curriculum learning, the training algorithm must resolve 2 problems: (i) sort the training examples by difficulty; (ii) compute a series of mini-batches that exhibit an increasing level of difficulty. We address challenge (i) using two methods: transfer learning from some competitive ``teacher" network, and bootstrapping. In our empirical evaluation, both methods show similar benefits in terms of increased learning speed and improved final performance on test data. We address challenge (ii) by investigating different pacing functions to guide the sampling. The empirical investigation includes a variety of network architectures, using images from CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and subsets of ImageNet. We conclude with a novel theoretical analysis of curriculum learning, where we show how it effectively modifies the optimization landscape. We then define the concept of an ideal curriculum, and show that under mild conditions it does not change the corresponding global minimum of the optimization function.
generated_abstract: We present an adaptive curriculum framework for end-to-end multilingual speech recognition that combines deep residual convolutional encoders, recurrent sequence modeling, cyclical learning rates, and learned data selection. A teacher agent dynamically constructs a syllabus over utterance difficulty, noise level, language, and label confidence, using learning progress and student performance to weight training examples. The curriculum begins with short, clean sequences and progressively introduces longer, noisier, accented, and cross-lingual utterances, while a reverse-generation strategy expands training from reliably decoded examples toward challenging cases. The student is trained with an efficient residualized encoder–decoder architecture, enabling substantially greater depth without compromising optimization. Evaluations on English and Mandarin speech under clean, noisy, and corrupted-label conditions demonstrate faster convergence, improved robustness, and better data efficiency than fixed curricula, conventional learning-rate schedules, and strong end-to-end baselines. The results show that jointly optimizing representation depth, optimization dynamics, and teaching strategy provides a practical route to scalable speech recognition in heterogeneous real-world environments.

original_abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks fostered a newfound interest in generative models, resulting in a swelling wave of new works that new-coming researchers may find formidable to surf. In this paper, we intend to help those researchers, by splitting that incoming wave into six "fronts": Architectural Contributions, Conditional Techniques, Normalization and Constraint Contributions, Loss Functions, Image-to-image Translations, and Validation Metrics. The division in fronts organizes literature into approachable blocks, ultimately communicating to the reader how the area is evolving. Previous surveys in the area, which this works also tabulates, focus on a few of those fronts, leaving a gap that we propose to fill with a more integrated, comprehensive overview. Here, instead of an exhaustive survey, we opt for a straightforward review: our target is to be an entry point to this vast literature, and also to be able to update experienced researchers to the newest techniques.
generated_abstract: We present a controllable, high-resolution generative framework for data augmentation and semantic image synthesis under limited annotation. Our approach combines conditional generation from semantic and instance-level maps with progressive growing, multi-scale adversarial discrimination, style-based latent control, and a least-squares adversarial objective to improve stability, fidelity, and diversity. A truncation mechanism provides an explicit trade-off between sample quality and variation, while disentangled style codes enable scale-specific manipulation of object appearance and scene attributes. The resulting model supports both realistic image generation and interactive editing, including object insertion, removal, category replacement, and appearance modification. We evaluate the framework on several natural-image benchmarks using distributional metrics, diversity and disentanglement measures, human perceptual studies, and downstream semi-supervised classification performance. Results demonstrate improved stability and high-resolution realism over conventional, conditional, and progressively trained GAN baselines, while generated samples substantially enhance recognition when labeled data are scarce. These findings show that integrating architectural, optimization, and latent-space design principles provides a practical foundation for controllable visual synthesis and effective augmentation in real-world computer-vision applications.

original_abstract: Local differential privacy (LDP) can provide each user with strong privacy guarantees under untrusted data curators while ensuring accurate statistics derived from privatized data. Due to its powerfulness, LDP has been widely adopted to protect privacy in various tasks (e.g., heavy hitters discovery, probability estimation) and systems (e.g., Google Chrome, Apple iOS). Although ${\epsilon}$-LDP has been proposed for many years, the more general notion of $({\epsilon}, {\delta})$-LDP has only been studied in very few papers, which mainly consider mean estimation for numeric data. Besides, prior solutions achieve $({\epsilon}, {\delta})$-LDP by leveraging Gaussian mechanism, which leads to low accuracy of the aggregated results. In this paper, we propose novel mechanisms that achieve $({\epsilon}, {\delta})$-LDP with high utility in data analytics and machine learning. Specifically, we first design $({\epsilon}, {\delta})$-LDP algorithms for collecting multi-dimensional numeric data, which can ensure higher accuracy than the optimal Gaussian mechanism while guaranteeing strong privacy for each user. Then, we investigate different local protocols for categorical attributes under $({\epsilon}, {\delta})$-LDP. Furthermore, we conduct theoretical analysis on the error bound and variance of the proposed algorithms. Experimental results on real and synthetic datasets demonstrate the high data utility of our proposed algorithms on both simple data statistics and complex machine learning models.
generated_abstract: We present a privacy-preserving analytics framework for smart-device applications that combines local differential privacy with accurate estimation and machine learning over heterogeneous user data. The framework supports numerical, categorical, marginal, and key-value attributes, enabling frequency and mean estimation, correlation analysis, regression, and deep-model training without exposing raw user records to the data collector. To address unbounded numerical data, we incorporate robust locally private Gaussian estimation, while Rényi differential privacy provides tight accounting for composed and iterative mechanisms. Utility is improved through analytically calibrated Gaussian perturbation, optimal or near-optimal local randomization, iterative key-value estimation, and post-processing denoising. We further develop privacy-aware stochastic optimization for linear, generalized linear, and neural models, and characterize accuracy through minimax estimation guarantees under local privacy constraints. Experiments on real and synthetic smart-device datasets show that the integrated design substantially improves statistical and predictive accuracy over conventional randomized-response and independently calibrated Gaussian baselines at comparable privacy levels, while preserving the client-side protection and scalability required for large-scale deployment.

original_abstract: We investigate the combination of actor-critic reinforcement learning algorithms with uniform large-scale experience replay and propose solutions for two challenges: (a) efficient actor-critic learning with experience replay (b) stability of very off-policy learning. We employ those insights to accelerate hyper-parameter sweeps in which all participating agents run concurrently and share their experience via a common replay module. To this end we analyze the bias-variance tradeoffs in V-trace, a form of importance sampling for actor-critic methods. Based on our analysis, we then argue for mixing experience sampled from replay with on-policy experience, and propose a new trust region scheme that scales effectively to data distributions where V-trace becomes unstable. We provide extensive empirical validation of the proposed solution. We further show the benefits of this setup by demonstrating state-of-the-art data efficiency on Atari among agents trained up until 200M environment frames.
generated_abstract: We present a scalable, sample-efficient reinforcement-learning architecture for visual, partially observable, and multi-task control. The system combines massively parallel actors with decoupled learners, prioritized sequence replay, and off-policy correction through truncated importance sampling and distributional Retrace updates. A recurrent actor–critic network integrates raw visual observations with auxiliary task features, while entropy regularization and trust-region policy updates improve exploration and optimization stability. Meta-gradients adapt discounting, trace parameters, and return construction online, allowing the agent to adjust its learning dynamics across tasks and levels of off-policyness. The architecture supports both discrete and continuous action spaces and can exploit experience collected by heterogeneous behavior policies. We evaluate the approach on Atari-style visual control, first-person navigation and combat, and continuous motor-control benchmarks, comparing data efficiency, wall-clock scalability, transfer, and robustness across random seeds. Ablation studies isolate the effects of distributed execution, prioritized replay, multi-step off-policy learning, adaptive returns, and auxiliary feature prediction. The resulting framework provides a unified application-oriented agent that combines the throughput of distributed deep reinforcement learning with the stability, exploration, and sample efficiency of modern off-policy actor–critic methods.

original_abstract: The design of deep graph models still remains to be investigated and the crucial part is how to explore and exploit the knowledge from different hops of neighbors in an efficient way. In this paper, we propose a novel RNN-like deep graph neural network architecture by incorporating AdaBoost into the computation of network; and the proposed graph convolutional network called AdaGCN~(AdaBoosting Graph Convolutional Network) has the ability to efficiently extract knowledge from high-order neighbors and integrate knowledge from different hops of neighbors into the network in an AdaBoost way. We also present the architectural difference between AdaGCN and existing graph convolutional methods to show the benefits of our proposal. Finally, extensive experiments demonstrate the state-of-the-art prediction performance and the computational advantage of our approach AdaGCN.
generated_abstract: We propose an adaptive multi-scale graph convolutional network for semi-supervised node classification on irregular graphs. The model combines localized spectral filtering with efficient neighborhood aggregation, attention-based weighting, and higher-order neighborhood mixing to capture both low-pass structural signals and discriminative relationships across multiple graph distances. To support deeper architectures, propagation and feature transformation are decoupled, while jumping-knowledge aggregation adaptively selects receptive-field sizes for each node, mitigating over-smoothing and graph-dependent variation in neighborhood structure. An expressive permutation-invariant aggregation module further improves the ability to distinguish local graph configurations, and optional linearized propagation enables substantial reductions in computational and memory costs. Experiments on citation, co-authorship, co-purchase, and protein-interaction benchmarks demonstrate improved accuracy and robustness under limited supervision and adversarial perturbations, while ablation studies quantify the contributions of spectral localization, attention, multi-scale mixing, and adaptive depth. The results show that combining complementary graph convolution principles yields an accurate, interpretable, and scalable framework for graph-based applications.

original_abstract: This paper seeks to answer a simple but fundamental question: what role can non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) play in massive multi-in multi-out (MIMO)? It is well established that power-domain NOMA schemes can outperform conventional orthogonal multiple access schemes in cellular networks. However, this fact does not imply that NOMA is the most efficient way to communicate in massive MIMO setups, where the base stations have many more antennas than there are users in the cell. These setups are becoming the norm in future networks and are usually studied by assuming spatial multiplexing of the users using linear multi-user beamforming. To answer the above-mentioned question, we analyze and compare the performance achieved by NOMA and multi-user beamforming in both non-line-of-sight and line-of-sight scenarios. We reveal that the latter scheme gives the highest average sum rate in massive MIMO setups. We also identify specific cases where NOMA is the better choice in massive MIMO and explain how NOMA plays an essential role in creating a hybrid of NOMA and multi-user beamforming that is shown to perform better than two standalone schemes do.
generated_abstract: This paper proposes a robust downlink application framework that combines TDD massive MIMO, low-feedback NOMA, and pilot-free effective-channel estimation for high-connectivity wireless systems. Excess antennas are exploited to spatially separate user clusters, while superposition coding and successive interference cancellation enable multiple users to share the same time-frequency resources. To reduce signaling overhead, user ordering and clustering rely on limited feedback, and terminals estimate their instantaneous effective channel gains blindly without downlink pilots. The performance is analyzed using ergodic-rate bounds selected according to the propagation regime, thereby accounting for both favorable propagation and scenarios with channel correlation, keyhole effects, or insufficient channel hardening. Joint power allocation and beamforming are formulated to balance inter-cluster interference, SIC reliability, and fairness under imperfect channel state information. Numerical evaluations show that the proposed design achieves higher spectral efficiency and user connectivity than orthogonal access and conventional pilot-based massive-MIMO-NOMA schemes, particularly when feedback, training resources, or channel hardening are limited. The results demonstrate that combining excess spatial degrees of freedom with nonorthogonal transmission and adaptive channel-gain acquisition provides an efficient and scalable solution for beyond-5G applications.

original_abstract: In [1, 2], we have explored the theoretical aspects of feature extraction optimization processes for solving largescale problems and overcoming machine learning limitations. Majority of optimization algorithms that have been introduced in [1, 2] guarantee the optimal performance of supervised learning, given offline and discrete data, to deal with curse of dimensionality (CoD) problem. These algorithms, however, are not tailored for solving emerging learning problems. One of the important issues caused by online data is lack of sufficient samples per class. Further, traditional machine learning algorithms cannot achieve accurate training based on limited distributed data, as data has proliferated and dispersed significantly. Machine learning employs a strict model or embedded engine to train and predict which still fails to learn unseen classes and sufficiently use online data. In this chapter, we introduce these challenges elaborately. We further investigate Meta-Learning (MTL) algorithm, and their application and promises to solve the emerging problems by answering how autonomous agents can learn to learn?.
generated_abstract: We present a robust few-shot learning framework for visual recognition that combines metric-based comparison, rapid gradient adaptation, synthetic data generation, and uncertainty modeling. The proposed method represents each class through support-set prototypes and learned relation scores, while a jointly trained hallucinator generates plausible feature-space examples to reduce the variance induced by extremely limited supervision. A probabilistic MAML++ adaptation module captures task ambiguity by producing a distribution of task-specific classifiers rather than a single estimate, and meta-transfer scaling and shifting enable efficient adaptation of deep feature extractors. Training uses hierarchical episodic curricula containing heterogeneous tasks, improving generalization to novel class structures and domains. At inference, predictions aggregate prototype distances and relation scores across sampled adapted models without full retraining. Experiments on standard low-shot image-classification benchmarks and cross-domain task splits show consistent improvements over prototypical, matching, relation-network, MAML, and hallucination-based baselines, particularly in the one-shot regime. Ablation studies demonstrate that synthetic support augmentation, probabilistic adaptation, and hierarchical task training provide complementary gains in accuracy, calibration, and computational efficiency.

original_abstract: Edge computing is an emerging concept based on distributing computing, storage, and control services closer to end network nodes. Edge computing lies at the heart of the fifth generation (5G) wireless systems and beyond. While current state-of-the-art networks communicate, compute, and process data in a centralized manner (at the cloud), for latency and compute-centric applications, both radio access and computational resources must be brought closer to the edge, harnessing the availability of computing and storage-enabled small cell base stations in proximity to the end devices. Furthermore, the network infrastructure must enable a distributed edge decision-making service that learns to adapt to the network dynamics with minimal latency and optimize network deployment and operation accordingly. This article will provide a fresh look to the concept of edge computing by first discussing the applications that the network edge must provide, with a special emphasis on the ensuing challenges in enabling ultra-reliable and low-latency edge computing services for mission-critical applications such as virtual reality (VR), vehicle-to-everything (V2X), edge artificial intelligence (AI), and so forth. Furthermore, several case studies where the edge is key are explored followed by insights and prospect for future work.
generated_abstract: This paper proposes an intelligent, mobility-aware edge computing framework for ultra-reliable low-latency applications in ultra-dense 5G and beyond networks. The framework jointly manages user association, dual connectivity, handover, task offloading, and radio–computational resource allocation across heterogeneous sub-6-GHz and millimeter-wave access points. To address intermittent blockage, dormant base stations, spatially and temporally correlated mobility, and dynamically varying workloads, a two-timescale design is developed. At the long timescale, mean-field and stochastic-geometric models determine energy-efficient user-centric associations and connectivity configurations, while matching-based decisions account for edge-server capabilities and queue states. At the short timescale, Lyapunov optimization dynamically allocates transmit power, bandwidth, and computing resources subject to probabilistic queue-length constraints derived from extreme-value theory. A lightweight edge-learning module further enables distributed prediction of mobility, blockage, and workload patterns using model exchange rather than raw data, thereby improving proactive handover and offloading decisions while preserving privacy. The proposed design explicitly captures the tradeoffs among energy consumption, inference and task latency, reliability, and signaling overhead. Numerical evaluations demonstrate substantial reductions in tail latency and service violations, improved resilience to millimeter-wave link failures, and higher energy efficiency than conventional handover, single-connectivity, and average-based MEC baselines.

original_abstract: Automatic Post-Editing (APE) aims to correct systematic errors in a machine translated text. This is primarily useful when the machine translation (MT) system is not accessible for improvement, leaving APE as a viable option to improve translation quality as a downstream task - which is the focus of this thesis. This field has received less attention compared to MT due to several reasons, which include: the limited availability of data to perform a sound research, contrasting views reported by different researchers about the effectiveness of APE, and limited attention from the industry to use APE in current production pipelines. In this thesis, we perform a thorough investigation of APE as a downstream task in order to: i) understand its potential to improve translation quality; ii) advance the core technology - starting from classical methods to recent deep-learning based solutions; iii) cope with limited and sparse data; iv) better leverage multiple input sources; v) mitigate the task-specific problem of over-correction; vi) enhance neural decoding to leverage external knowledge; and vii) establish an online learning framework to handle data diversity in real-time. All the above contributions are discussed across several chapters, and most of them are evaluated in the APE shared task organized each year at the Conference on Machine Translation. Our efforts in improving the technology resulted in the best system at the 2017 APE shared task, and our work on online learning received a distinguished paper award at the Italian Conference on Computational Linguistics. Overall, outcomes and findings of our work have boost interest among researchers and attracted industries to examine this technology to solve real-word problems.
generated_abstract: We present an adaptive, quality-aware neural automatic post-editing framework that combines source–translation attention, multi-source Transformer encoding, specialized factored models, and log-linear reranking. The system jointly exploits the original source sentence, the machine-translated hypothesis, and word-level quality-estimation signals to identify likely errors while preserving reliable content. Alignment-guided attention supports targeted corrections, whereas a copy and edit-conservatism objective reduces overcorrection and maintains fidelity to the input translation. Multiple complementary post-editing and language models are combined through tuned log-linear decoding, with synthetic error–correction data addressing the limited availability of human post-edits. Finally, post-edited hypotheses and quality predictions are used for confidence-aware selection and online adaptation from newly approved edits. Experiments across machine-translation outputs of varying quality evaluate translation improvement, edit reduction, and word- and sentence-level quality estimation. The proposed framework is designed to unify correction, confidence assessment, and continual learning in a portable second-stage system that improves translation quality while reducing human post-editing effort.

original_abstract: We consider a variant of the classic Ski Rental online algorithm with applications to machine learning. In our variant, we allow the skier access to a black-box machine-learning algorithm that provides an estimate of the probability that there will be at most a threshold number of ski-days. We derive a class of optimal randomized algorithms to determine the strategy that minimizes the worst-case expected competitive ratio for the skier given a prediction from the machine learning algorithm,and analyze the performance and robustness of these algorithms.
generated_abstract: We study prediction-augmented online monetization for ad platforms that must jointly set reserve prices and manage limited reusable resources such as cached creatives or edge capacity. We combine bid prediction under squared loss with robust online decision-making, treating learned forecasts as black-box advice rather than assumptions that must always be trusted. Our algorithms interpolate between prediction-driven policies and classical worst-case strategies: accurate forecasts yield improved revenue and reduced operational cost, while inaccurate forecasts incur only bounded degradation and retain logarithmic-style competitive guarantees. We further develop an average-case analysis showing that, under realistic demand distributions, the optimal policy may rationally follow predictions more aggressively than worst-case analysis permits, while still maintaining robustness through adaptive fallback thresholds. The resulting framework provides explicit performance bounds in terms of prediction error and distributional parameters, and applies to both reserve-price selection and cache eviction. Experiments on auction and request-trace datasets demonstrate that the proposed policies consistently outperform prediction-free baselines and naive reliance on forecasts, particularly when prediction quality varies across opportunity types.

original_abstract: While deep learning (DL)-based networked systems have shown great potential in various applications, a key drawback is that Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) in DL are blackboxes and nontransparent for network operators. The lack of interpretability makes DL-based networked systems challenging to operate and troubleshoot, which further prevents DL-based networked systems from deploying in practice. In this paper, we propose TranSys, a novel framework to explain DL-based networked systems for practical deployment. Transys categorizes current DL-based networked systems and introduces different explanation methods based on decision tree and hypergraph to effectively explain DL-based networked systems. TranSys can explain the DNN policies in the form of decision trees and highlight critical components based on analysis over hypergraph. We evaluate TranSys over several typical DL-based networked systems and demonstrate that Transys can provide human-readable explanations for network operators. We also present three use cases of Transys, which could (i) help network operators troubleshoot DL-based networked systems, (ii) improve the decision latency and resource consumption of DL-based networked systems by ~10x on different metrics, and (iii) provide suggestions on daily operations for network operators when incidences occur.
generated_abstract: We present an explainable and verifiable learning framework for self-driving network management that combines graph neural network modeling, reinforcement-learning-based optimization, and post hoc interpretability. The framework represents topology, routing, traffic, and operational state as graph-structured inputs; predicts performance measures such as delay and jitter; and selects routing or packet-processing actions using learned policies optimized for latency, memory, and reliability. To expose model behavior, we integrate local subgraph and feature explanations with additive feature attribution, hidden-representation analysis, and systematic input exploration. These explanations identify the links, flows, traffic conditions, and latent concepts that drive individual decisions, while formal neural-network verification checks whether learned policies satisfy administrator-specified safety and performance constraints over defined operating regions. Evaluated on unseen topologies, routing schemes, traffic conditions, and rule sets, the approach preserves the generalization and optimization benefits of learned network models while revealing failure modes and supporting diagnosis, refinement, and trustworthy deployment. This application demonstrates how interpretability and verification can transform accurate but opaque network-learning components into auditable building blocks for autonomous networking.

original_abstract: This paper proposes the first model-free Reinforcement Learning (RL) framework to synthesise policies for unknown, and continuous-state Markov Decision Processes (MDPs), such that a given linear temporal property is satisfied. We convert the given property into a Limit Deterministic Buchi Automaton (LDBA), namely a finite-state machine expressing the property. Exploiting the structure of the LDBA, we shape a synchronous reward function on-the-fly, so that an RL algorithm can synthesise a policy resulting in traces that probabilistically satisfy the linear temporal property. This probability (certificate) is also calculated in parallel with policy learning when the state space of the MDP is finite: as such, the RL algorithm produces a policy that is certified with respect to the property. Under the assumption of finite state space, theoretical guarantees are provided on the convergence of the RL algorithm to an optimal policy, maximising the above probability. We also show that our method produces ''best available'' control policies when the logical property cannot be satisfied. In the general case of a continuous state space, we propose a neural network architecture for RL and we empirically show that the algorithm finds satisfying policies, if there exist such policies. The performance of the proposed framework is evaluated via a set of numerical examples and benchmarks, where we observe an improvement of one order of magnitude in the number of iterations required for the policy synthesis, compared to existing approaches whenever available.
generated_abstract: We present a safety-critical reinforcement learning framework for autonomous navigation in heterogeneous, partially unknown environments. The approach combines temporal-logic-based product construction, permissive safety synthesis, adaptive shielding, and model-free value learning to optimize an unknown performance objective while preserving probabilistic guarantees for Linear Temporal Logic specifications. A verification-preserving model-update mechanism maintains safety when observations falsify or refine the currently trusted environmental model, while specification-guided exploration restricts learning to behaviors relevant to task satisfaction. The resulting policy is synthesized online without requiring a complete transition model and achieves a tunable trade-off between exploration efficiency and strict safety. We establish that the shield prevents specification-violating actions with high probability under the maintained model set and that, under standard learning assumptions, the learned policy asymptotically approaches the best policy within the safe operating envelope; finite-sample performance bounds are provided for the model-based variant. Experiments on simulated mobile-robot missions with uncertain maps, stochastic motion, and changing obstacles demonstrate substantially fewer unsafe interactions and faster convergence than unconstrained and single-model reinforcement-learning baselines, while retaining competitive task performance.

original_abstract: Many inferential and learning tasks can be accomplished efficiently by means of distributed optimization algorithms where the network topology plays a critical role in driving the local interactions among neighboring agents. There is a large body of literature examining the effect of the graph structure on the performance of optimization strategies. In this article, we examine the inverse problem and consider the reverse question: How much information does observing the behavior at the nodes convey about the underlying network structure used for optimization? Over large-scale networks, the difficulty of addressing such inverse questions (or problems) is compounded by the fact that usually only a limited portion of nodes can be probed, giving rise to a second important question: Despite the presence of several unobserved nodes, are partial and local observations still sufficient to discover the graph linking the probed nodes? The article surveys recent advances on this inverse learning problem and related questions. Examples of applications are provided to illustrate how the interplay between graph learning and distributed optimization arises in practice, e.g., in cognitive engineered systems such as distributed detection, or in other real-world problems such as the mechanism of opinion formation over social networks and the mechanism of coordination in biological networks. A unifying framework for examining the reconstruction error will be described, which allows to devise and examine various estimation strategies enabling successful graph learning. The relevance of specific network attributes, such as sparsity versus density of connections, and node degree concentration, is discussed in relation to the topology inference goal. It is shown how universal (i.e., data-driven) clustering algorithms can be exploited to solve the graph learning problem.
generated_abstract: We propose a unified framework for learning the local interaction structure of large diffusion and consensus networks from stationary signals observed at only a subset of agents. The method combines covariance-based characterization of graph diffusion with tomography from indirect, adaptive outputs. In particular, spectral information extracted from stationary observations defines a convex set of graph operators compatible with the data, while lagged correlations and residual statistics provide node-pair scores for distinguishing direct interactions among observed agents. A clustering and convex-selection procedure then recovers a sparse, interpretable subgraph without requiring knowledge of the total network size or assuming global sparsity. We establish consistency under partial and low observability when the latent network follows an Erdős–Rényi model, showing that concentration of latent node degrees creates an identifiability gap between interacting and noninteracting pairs, including in dense regimes. The framework accommodates symmetric consensus dynamics and asymmetric adaptive combination policies, thereby supporting structural and causal interpretations. Experiments on synthetic networks and temperature-sensing data demonstrate accurate local topology recovery, robustness to observation noise and finite time horizons, and improved performance over correlation-, Granger-, and sparsity-based baselines.

original_abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) has recently led to many breakthroughs on a range of complex control tasks. However, the agent's decision-making process is generally not transparent. The lack of interpretability hinders the applicability of RL in safety-critical scenarios. While several methods have attempted to interpret vision-based RL, most come without detailed explanation for the agent's behaviour. In this paper, we propose a self-supervised interpretable framework, which can discover causal features to enable easy interpretation of RL agents even for non-experts. Specifically, a self-supervised interpretable network (SSINet) is employed to produce fine-grained attention masks for highlighting task-relevant information, which constitutes most evidence for the agent's decisions. We verify and evaluate our method on several Atari 2600 games as well as Duckietown, which is a challenging self-driving car simulator environment. The results show that our method renders causal explanations and empirical evidences about how the agent makes decisions and why the agent performs well or badly, especially when transferred to novel scenes. Overall, our method provides valuable insight into the internal decision-making process of vision-based RL. In addition, our method does not use any external labelled data, and thus demonstrates the possibility to learn high-quality mask through a self-supervised manner, which may shed light on new paradigms for label-free vision learning such as self-supervised segmentation and detection.
generated_abstract: We present an interpretable attention-augmented dueling deep Q-network that combines recurrent state modeling, self-supervised multi-focus attention, and model-agnostic perturbation explanations for visual reinforcement learning. The architecture decomposes action values into state-value and advantage components while using an attention bottleneck to identify task-relevant spatial and semantic regions over time, supporting decision making under partial observability. Unlike purely architectural visualizations, the proposed framework evaluates attention maps through meaningful perturbations that directly measure their influence on action selection and value estimates. We apply the method to Atari 2600 environments and analyze learning dynamics, emergent strategies, temporal shifts in attention, and failure cases. The resulting explanations reveal whether agents attend to behaviorally relevant objects, distinguish spatial “where” from semantic “what” information, and expose reliance on superficial trajectory-specific features. Across games, the model achieves competitive or improved performance relative to conventional and dueling DQN baselines while incurring minimal computational overhead. These results demonstrate that integrating interpretable attention with value decomposition can provide faithful, actionable explanations without sacrificing reinforcement-learning performance.

original_abstract: Concolic testing is a test generation technique which works effectively by integrating random testing generation and symbolic execution. Existing concolic testing engines focus on numeric programs. Heap-manipulating programs make extensive use of complex heap objects like trees and lists. Testing such programs is challenging due to multiple reasons. Firstly, test inputs for such program are required to satisfy non-trivial constraints which must be specified precisely. Secondly, precisely encoding and solving path conditions in such programs are challenging and often expensive. In this work, we propose the first concolic testing engine called CSF for heap-manipulating programs based on separation logic. CSF effectively combines specification-based testing and concolic execution for test input generation. It is evaluated on a set of challenging heap-manipulating programs. The results show that CSF generates valid test inputs with high coverage efficiently. Furthermore, we show that CSF can be potentially used in combination with precondition inference tools to reduce the user effort.
generated_abstract: We present a hybrid framework for automated testing and verification of JavaScript programs that combines compositional symbolic execution, separation-logic-based heap reasoning, and search-guided fuzzing. The framework uses bi-abduction and context-sensitive lazy initialization to infer precise heap resources and generate fully initialized, valid inputs, while user-defined shape, size, and bag predicates express structural and data-oriented properties of complex structures. Search-based generation produces legal sequences of API calls for constructing heap inputs, and selective symbolic execution is invoked only when fuzzing fails to cross path constraints, reducing path explosion while reaching deeper program behaviors. Symbolic execution errors and inferred preconditions provide actionable feedback and guide both input construction and exploration. A modular meta-theory, grounded in coherent logical structure, supports the sound integration of compositional reasoning with hybrid testing. We implement the approach as an extension of JaVerT 2.0 and evaluate it on JavaScript data-structure libraries and programs with complex heap inputs, measuring validity, coverage, scalability, and vulnerability-discovery effectiveness. The results demonstrate that combining precise separation-logic reasoning with search and fuzzing substantially reduces invalid tests, improves deep-path coverage, and enables practical compositional testing of heap-manipulating applications.

original_abstract: Prior work on controllable text generation usually assumes that the controlled attribute can take on one of a small set of values known a priori. In this work, we propose a novel task, where the syntax of a generated sentence is controlled rather by a sentential exemplar. To evaluate quantitatively with standard metrics, we create a novel dataset with human annotations. We also develop a variational model with a neural module specifically designed for capturing syntactic knowledge and several multitask training objectives to promote disentangled representation learning. Empirically, the proposed model is observed to achieve improvements over baselines and learn to capture desirable characteristics.
generated_abstract: We present a controllable exemplar-guided text generation framework that combines hierarchical variational representations, disentangled syntax–semantics and style factors, and prototype-based editing. Given an input sentence and desired attributes, the model retrieves a semantically related prototype, encodes content, syntax, style, and discourse intent into separate latent variables, and generates an output by editing the prototype through a multi-level decoder. Auxiliary paraphrase, bag-of-words, adversarial, and attribute-prediction objectives encourage content preservation, interpretable factorization, and reliable control, while exemplar conditioning improves fluency and reduces repetition in long outputs. The framework supports diverse paraphrase generation, non-parallel style transfer, and controllable expansion of short inputs without requiring parallel supervision. Experiments across these applications show improved attribute accuracy, semantic preservation, syntactic flexibility, diversity, and human-rated coherence over conventional variational, encoder–decoder, and exemplar-based baselines. Latent-space interpolation and targeted edits further demonstrate that the learned representations enable interpretable manipulation of sentence meaning, phrasing, and discourse-level realization.

original_abstract: Hyperspectral images (HSI) provide rich spectral information that contributed to the successful performance improvement of numerous computer vision tasks. However, it can only be achieved at the expense of images' spatial resolution. Hyperspectral image super-resolution (HSI-SR) addresses this problem by fusing low resolution (LR) HSI with multispectral image (MSI) carrying much higher spatial resolution (HR). All existing HSI-SR approaches require the LR HSI and HR MSI to be well registered and the reconstruction accuracy of the HR HSI relies heavily on the registration accuracy of different modalities. This paper exploits the uncharted problem domain of HSI-SR without the requirement of multi-modality registration. Given the unregistered LR HSI and HR MSI with overlapped regions, we design a unique unsupervised learning structure linking the two unregistered modalities by projecting them into the same statistical space through the same encoder. The mutual information (MI) is further adopted to capture the non-linear statistical dependencies between the representations from two modalities (carrying spatial information) and their raw inputs. By maximizing the MI, spatial correlations between different modalities can be well characterized to further reduce the spectral distortion. A collaborative $l_{2,1}$ norm is employed as the reconstruction error instead of the more common $l_2$ norm, so that individual pixels can be recovered as accurately as possible. With this design, the network allows to extract correlated spectral and spatial information from unregistered images that better preserves the spectral information. The proposed method is referred to as unregistered and unsupervised mutual Dirichlet Net ($u^2$-MDN). Extensive experimental results using benchmark HSI datasets demonstrate the superior performance of $u^2$-MDN as compared to the state-of-the-art.
generated_abstract: We propose an unsupervised model-based deep residual network for high-resolution hyperspectral image reconstruction from a low-resolution hyperspectral image and a high-resolution multispectral or RGB observation. The method combines the spatial–spectral representation capability of coupled convolutional networks with the accuracy and optimization stability of residual learning. An unfolded fusion module explicitly incorporates the spatial degradation and spectral response models, while adaptive convolutional layers jointly estimate the point spread and spectral response functions when sensor calibration is unavailable. To preserve material signatures, the network employs shared latent representations with sparse spectral coding, angular spectral consistency, and a spatial reconstruction constraint. A lightweight convolutional super-resolution branch further refines high-frequency structures transferred from the guidance image without introducing spectral artifacts. The entire architecture is trained using only the observed low-resolution hyperspectral and high-resolution multispectral images, eliminating the need for high-resolution hyperspectral ground truth. Experiments on simulated and real datasets demonstrate improved spatial detail, spectral fidelity, and robustness to unknown sensor characteristics compared with conventional pansharpening, supervised deep networks, and existing unsupervised fusion methods. The proposed framework provides an efficient and transferable solution for remote-sensing applications requiring high-quality hyperspectral products under practical acquisition constraints.

original_abstract: This paper presents SimCLR: a simple framework for contrastive learning of visual representations. We simplify recently proposed contrastive self-supervised learning algorithms without requiring specialized architectures or a memory bank. In order to understand what enables the contrastive prediction tasks to learn useful representations, we systematically study the major components of our framework. We show that (1) composition of data augmentations plays a critical role in defining effective predictive tasks, (2) introducing a learnable nonlinear transformation between the representation and the contrastive loss substantially improves the quality of the learned representations, and (3) contrastive learning benefits from larger batch sizes and more training steps compared to supervised learning. By combining these findings, we are able to considerably outperform previous methods for self-supervised and semi-supervised learning on ImageNet. A linear classifier trained on self-supervised representations learned by SimCLR achieves 76.5% top-1 accuracy, which is a 7% relative improvement over previous state-of-the-art, matching the performance of a supervised ResNet-50. When fine-tuned on only 1% of the labels, we achieve 85.8% top-5 accuracy, outperforming AlexNet with 100X fewer labels.
generated_abstract: We present a unified self-supervised framework for data-efficient visual recognition that combines geometric pretext tasks, context and spatial-structure prediction, contrastive predictive coding, and multi-view mutual-information maximization. A momentum-updated encoder and dynamic feature queue provide stable large-scale instance discrimination, while local aggregation encourages semantically coherent neighborhoods and transformation-based objectives preserve spatially meaningful features. We further incorporate architecture and augmentation choices identified as critical for self-supervised learning. Pretraining requires only unlabeled images and produces representations that are both invariant to appearance changes and sensitive to object structure and context. Across linear evaluation, few-shot classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation, the proposed combination consistently improves label efficiency over individual objectives and supervised initialization, particularly when annotations are scarce. These results demonstrate that complementary self-supervised signals can be integrated into a practical representation-learning pipeline that narrows the gap between unsupervised and fully supervised visual perception.

original_abstract: Existing analysis work in machine reading comprehension (MRC) is largely concerned with evaluating the capabilities of systems. However, the capabilities of datasets are not assessed for benchmarking language understanding precisely. We propose a semi-automated, ablation-based methodology for this challenge; By checking whether questions can be solved even after removing features associated with a skill requisite for language understanding, we evaluate to what degree the questions do not require the skill. Experiments on 10 datasets (e.g., CoQA, SQuAD v2.0, and RACE) with a strong baseline model show that, for example, the relative scores of a baseline model provided with content words only and with shuffled sentence words in the context are on average 89.2% and 78.5% of the original score, respectively. These results suggest that most of the questions already answered correctly by the model do not necessarily require grammatical and complex reasoning. For precise benchmarking, MRC datasets will need to take extra care in their design to ensure that questions can correctly evaluate the intended skills.
generated_abstract: We present a robust conversational reading-comprehension framework that integrates extractive and generative question answering, multi-sentence reasoning, adversarial robustness, and explicit abstention. Building on SQuAD, SQuAD 2.0, CoQA, DuoRC, ARC, and multi-sentence challenge sets, our application is designed to answer context-dependent questions across heterogeneous documents while handling coreference, paraphrase, external knowledge, and unsupported queries. The system jointly encodes conversational history and passage structure, retrieves and aggregates evidence across sentences, predicts free-form or span-based answers, and estimates whether sufficient evidence exists to abstain. We evaluate it using standard and adversarially perturbed passages, paraphrased documents, unanswerable questions, and science-oriented reasoning tasks. In addition to answer accuracy and lexical-overlap metrics, we measure evidence sufficiency, calibration, robustness, and sensitivity to passage-only and question-only shortcuts. This unified evaluation exposes failures concealed by conventional benchmarks and provides a practical test of whether improvements reflect genuine language understanding rather than superficial cues.

original_abstract: Spatio-temporal action localization is a challenging yet fascinating task that aims to detect and classify human actions in video clips. In this paper, we develop a high-level video understanding module which can encode interactions between actors and objects both in space and time. In our formulation, spatio-temporal relationships are learned by performing self-attention operations on a graph structure connecting entities from consecutive clips. Noticeably, the use of graph learning is unprecedented for this task. From a computational point of view, the proposed module is backbone independent by design and does not need end-to-end training. When tested on the AVA dataset, it demonstrates a 10-16% relative mAP improvement over the baseline. Further, it can outperform or bring performances comparable to state-of-the-art models which require heavy end-to-end and synchronized training on multiple GPUs. Code is publicly available at: this https URL.
generated_abstract: We present a unified multiscale spatiotemporal network for video action recognition and localization that combines complementary advances in appearance–motion modeling, temporal resolution, and efficient 3D convolution. The architecture employs a SlowFast backbone, with a low-rate pathway capturing semantic context and a lightweight high-rate pathway preserving fine-grained motion, while factorized R(2+1)D residual blocks enable effective spatiotemporal representation learning. To promote interaction between modalities and views, we introduce a collaborative fusion module that shares convolutional parameters across spatial and temporal projections and learns their relative contributions. Long-term temporal convolutions further extend the receptive field to model complete action instances rather than short snippets. For untrimmed videos, multiscale features generate candidate action tubes that are linked through a temporally consistent association module, yielding joint recognition and localization in an end-to-end framework. The resulting model integrates appearance, motion, and long-range dynamics while reducing redundant computation, providing an interpretable and efficient solution for robust video action analysis.

original_abstract: Low bit-width integer weights and activations are very important for efficient inference, especially with respect to lower power consumption. We propose Monte Carlo methods to quantize the weights and activations of pre-trained neural networks without any re-training. By performing importance sampling we obtain quantized low bit-width integer values from full-precision weights and activations. The precision, sparsity, and complexity are easily configurable by the amount of sampling performed. Our approach, called Monte Carlo Quantization (MCQ), is linear in both time and space, with the resulting quantized, sparse networks showing minimal accuracy loss when compared to the original full-precision networks. Our method either outperforms or achieves competitive results on multiple benchmarks compared to previous quantization methods that do require additional training.
generated_abstract: We present a unified low-precision training and inference framework for deploying deep neural networks on resource-constrained edge devices. The method combines learned ternary weights and quantizers with stochastic local reparameterization, while representing activations, gradients, and error signals using low-bitwidth integers. Full-precision shadow parameters are maintained only during optimization, whereas forward and backward propagation use bitwise operations, shifts, and accumulations. Trainable scaling factors and thresholds adapt the discrete representations to each layer, improving expressive capacity over binary networks without sacrificing hardware efficiency. Batch normalization and other non-integer operations are replaced with fixed-point-compatible transformations to enable an end-to-end integer dataflow. Across image-classification benchmarks and representative edge-oriented architectures, the proposed approach substantially reduces model storage, multiplication count, and training and inference energy while maintaining accuracy close to full-precision baselines and consistently improving over fixed quantization and binary-weight methods. These results demonstrate a practical path toward energy-efficient on-device learning, including transfer and continual-learning scenarios, using programmable integer and neuromorphic hardware.

original_abstract: The advent of deep learning has given rise to neural scene representations - learned mathematical models of a 3D environment.
